Q: Delphi, hooking TBitmap.Create & stack trace A:

This should have been posted as a Technical Q&A question, not as Advice.

In any case, a class's constructor is not a standard function that you should be hooking directly. Besides, your hook's signature is wrong anyway. A constructor actually has 2 hidden parameters, not 1 as you assumed:

  • Self, which points at a class type or an object instance, depending on what the constructor is being called on.

  • DoAlloc, which tells the constructor whether or not to call TObject.NewInstance() to allocate memory for the new object before then initializing the object's data.

So, you need to update your definition of TBitmapCreateFunc, eg:

type
 TBitmapCreateFunc = function(Self: Pointer; DoAlloc: ShortInt): Pointer;

...

function Hook_TBitmap_Create(Self: Pointer; DoAlloc: ShortInt): Pointer;
var
  ...
begin
  ...
  Result := TBitmap_Create_Hook(Self, DoAlloc);  // Call original constructor
end;

However, because of this, you might consider hooking the class's virtual AfterConstruction() method instead of the constructor directly. AfterConstruction() is called after the constructor exits.

Q: What does Kubernetes actually do? A:

If your app needs an entire server to itself, you probably wouldn’t use kubernetes.

If you have a few different apps, and you want to run them on a fleet of machines (with each host running several different workloads at once), and you want to handle fluctuating pulses in workload (traffic) by dynamically scaling the number of copies of each app independently, then you have the use-case to appreciate kubernetes.

Kubernetes is an open source way to facilitate automatically scaling the number of copies of each app, allocating copies to particular hosts (accounting for resource requirements and available capacity), dynamically routing outside traffic to these app instances, testing for nonresponsive copies and routing traffic around them (and resetting them if they stay nonresponsive), connecting network storage volumes to specific hosts where an app needs it, dynamically maintaining internal DNS (and container IPs) to simplify communication between microservices, securely distributing credentials between containers (helping limit the scope so that it is difficult for one compromised app to escalate and impact others), and providing standardised tools and configuration to administer all of this.

Kubernetes is oriented towards avoiding outages of production services, by using redundancy to facilitate rolling maintenance and failure tolerance, and scaling to accomodate traffic surges.

Kubernetes is composed of many interchangeable components with narrow functions (similar to the UNIX philosophy). Perhaps the central component is a representation of the current and target state of the cluster, held in a distributed cache and manipulated (by other components) through an API microservice. This may be hosted on master nodes, along with components for allocating containers among worker node hosts, and components for various other control loops that monitor the cluster and perturb it towards the target state. There is a CLI tool for inputting the target state from configuration manifests. There is software that runs on each worker node (including the runtime for containers, drivers for cluster networking and network storage, and a client service for coordinating with the master nodes). There is also an ecosystem of related software, such as tools for packaging complex app deployments, or for improving observability of all workloads running on the cluster.

Some cloud vendors may also offer proprietary equivalents to Kubernetes, for example AWS ECS performs a similar role. Note that Kubernetes is for containerised services, and that for RESTful web services each container image must include its own web server to listen for and handle request traffic. This contrasts with platforms that handle the network connections and translate directly to function invocations, such as inetd, CGI or AWS Lambda.

Q: BigQuery: How to replace 0 with NULL in a FLOAT64 column during a SELECT statement? A:

I'm not a BigQuery user, but my reading of the error message is that it's saying your Sales column is INT64 while the 0 is being interpreted as a FLOAT64 literal; I feel the error message is slightly misleading because many people would assume that because INT64 and FLOAT64 are both numeric types that the query-engine could paper-over the problem with implicit conversions (which would likely succeed in this situation as all INT64 values can be (lossy) converted to FLOAT64.

If you're okay with keeping my_project.my_dataset.my_table.Sales as INT64 then the solution is to prod the query-parser into interpreting 0 as INT64 and not FLOAT64 using a CAST expression, so try this:

SELECT 
    t.Date,
    NULLIF( t.Sales, CAST(0 AS INT64) ) AS Sales_Cleaned
FROM
    my_project.my_dataset.my_table AS t

Alternatively, you can use a CASE expression, which some people might prefer:

SELECT 
    t.Date,
    ( CASE t.Sales WHEN 0 THEN NULL ELSE t.Sales END ) AS Sales_Cleaned
FROM
    my_project.my_dataset.my_table AS t
